extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in poetics
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance poetics treatise defending poetry and describing the qualities that make a poet and poetic works effective: their moral purpose, modes, and stylistic requirements. Gives criteria for kinds (pastoral, tragedy, comedy, etc.), the poet’s functions, and why poetry excels over philosophy and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet’s defining note: feigning notable images with delightful teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is known by 'feigning notable images of virtues, vices, or what else, with that delightful teaching' — i.e., making imagined representations that both delight and instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sidney emphasizes that the poet's craft is to invent images that teach virtue and vice while giving pleasure. This distinguishes the poet from mere talkers; the poet should combine invention with moral instruction rather than simple rhetoric or sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse as the fitting raiment: form suited to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'senate of poets have chosen verse as their fittest raiment' and do 'piece each syllable of each word by just proportion, according to the dignity of the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry's form (meter, diction, rhythm) must be appropriate to the subject's dignity — not conversational or dreamy speech. Attention to prosody and measured language is essential; avoid slack, table-talk phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final end of learning: lead to virtuous action (praxis)
rubrics_metrics.description: All earthly learning's 'ending end' is virtuous action; poetry's highest value lies in moving people toward virtuous practice, not merely knowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry by its capacity to produce moral effects in readers — not just to convey knowledge. The poet should aim for 'praxis' (action) as the fruit of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet couples the general with the particular (universal + example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'giveth a perfect picture' by presupposing a particular agent who exemplifies what the philosopher names in the abstract, thus coupling the general notion with the particular example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong poem translates abstract precepts into concrete images/characters that embody the general truth, making the general comprehensible and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of the 'perfect picture' to illuminate imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet 'yieldeth to the powers of the mind an image' that strikes, pierces, and possesses the sight of the soul more than wordish philosophical description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work creates vivid, convincing images that allow readers to 'see' a moral or character directly (analogy of painted elephant vs verbal description). The imaginative picture must be vivid enough to be grasped without further description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigned (invented) examples can instruct more than strict history
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, dealing with the universal, can frame feigned examples tuned to teach what should be done — sometimes more instructive and safer than literal historical examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value fictional examples that are shaped to illuminate causes, consequences, and moral lessons (e.g., Xenophon's feigned Cyrus vs historian's mere 'was'). Fictionalization is permitted and often preferable when it clarifies universal lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s philosophic reach: deals with the universal (καθολου)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Aristotle: 'poesy dealeth with καθολου, that is to say, with the universal consideration,' whereas history treats particulars (καθ ἔκαστον).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetry by its treatment of universal truths and likelihood/necessity rather than literal factual accuracy. The poet's truth is general applicability and insight into human behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must move (emotionally) as well as teach
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving is of a higher degree than teaching; nobody will be taught unless first moved with desire to be taught — poetry must incite desire and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems on their emotional power to motivate readers toward the taught ends. Rhetorical clarity without affective force is insufficient for moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and popular appeal: the poet as 'right popular philosopher'
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is 'the food for the tenderest stomachs' and 'the right popular philosopher' — able to instruct those whom abstract philosophy cannot reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poem's ability to convey moral instruction to broad and less-schooled audiences (children, common people) without sacrificing depth. Use of simple tales, allegory, and fable (Aesop, parables) is praiseworthy when it teaches effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight, musicality, and tale-structure as pedagogic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'cometh to you with words set in delightful proportion, either accompanied with, or prepared for, the well-enchanting skill of music; and with a tale' — delight and melody help win the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should be pleasurable (sonorous, proportioned), and narrative structure (a tale) often aids instruction. Evaluate the harmony of sound, rhythm, and narrative form as instruments of persuasion and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional integrity: parts and mixtures must each be good
rubrics_metrics.description: Some poesies couple kinds (tragical and comical, prose and verse); 'if severed they be good, the conjunction cannot be hurtful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When genres or modes are mixed, appraise the quality of each part individually; a successful hybrid requires each component to be well-executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral can instruct on social misery and contentment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral verse ('the poor pipe') can 'show the misery of people under hard lords' and depict the blessedness derived from good rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss pastoral as trivial: it can compress political and social lessons into simple rural imagery that reveals abuses and virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegy: evoke pity and rightly accompany lament
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'lamenting elegiac... would move rather pity than blame' and is praiseworthy for compassionately accompanying just causes of lamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate elegiac poetry by its capacity for sincere, proportionate mourning that highlights human weakness and prompts reflection, not mere melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iambic (invective) as corrective: 'rub the galled mind'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'bitter, but wholesome iambic... rubs the galled mind, making shame the trumpet of villany' — its sharpness corrects vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess invective/ iambic verse by its moral usefulness in shaming vice and provoking reform, rather than mere scorn or crude abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: expose folly through friendly mockery
rubrics_metrics.description: Satiric verse 'Omne vafer vitium ridenti tangit amico' — it makes a man laugh at folly and then ashamed of it, provoking self-recognition and correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good satire should touch faults with a smiling, knowing tone that leads readers to self-censure and reform; evaluate whether the satire produces constructive insight rather than merely humiliating its target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: imitation of common errors that discourages vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy 'is an imitation of the common errors of our life... so as it is impossible that any beholder can be content to be such a one' — the comic exposes follies to discourage them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comic works on their ability to render characters' foibles recognizably ridiculous, prompting audiences to avoid such behavior. Sidney rejects the notion that seeing vice onstage teaches evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: move admiration and pity to teach the world's uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'openeth the greatest wounds... with stirring the effects of admiration and commiseration, teacheth the uncertainty of this world,' and can soften even hard hearts (example: Alexander Pheræus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tragedy by its capacity to produce catharsis — strong pity and fear leading to moral reflection — and by its skill in exposing the consequences of pride and tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric/ode: praise virtue and kindle courage
rubrics_metrics.description: The lyric with 'tuned lyre and well-accorded voice, giveth praise, the reward of virtue... sometimes raiseth up his voice to the height of the heavens' and can awaken courage and noble enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess songs and odes on their capacity to celebrate virtuous acts and rouse communal or personal emulation (Pindaric example). Beware faults of time/custom, not of the genre itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical: the highest and most instructive kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical 'teacheth and moveth to the most high and excellent truth' and 'informs with counsel how to be worthy' by presenting loftiest examples (Æneas, Achilles, Cyrus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge epic/heroic poetry by its ability to present comprehensive models of virtuous conduct across varied circumstances (war, peace, private inward life), supplying exemplary counsels for imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should set virtue in its best colours (fortune as handmaid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'ever sets virtue so out in her best colours, making fortune her well-waiting handmaid' so readers are enamoured of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem elevates virtuous action by arranging plot and fortune to make virtue appear desirable and exemplary, rather than portraying virtue as unattractive or futile.
